description: Hello, we're looking for motivated individuals looking to win!
summary:
Emberline is a free tool and open data pipeline which harmonises the two generations of NASA's fire satellites MODIS (2000+) and VIIRS (2012+). Fires appear much more active when combining these satellite products together, as VIIRS can detect smaller and cooler fires than MODIS. Treating raw VIIRS counts as MODIS counts inflated estimated fire activity by 44–296% across the eight study areas.  In some areas the naive combination flips a decreasing trend to increasing.


We developed a model to predict what MODIS would have seen, and tested it on years and locations it was not trained on. The model has an overall error for estimating annual totals of 8.0%. This compares to an error of 11.5% for estimating a seasonal scaling factor and 124% for the naive combination. An independent remodelling achieved identical results for all 148 comparisons. Users can explore a 3D globe, and look at any county/area of interest. They can see a burning calendar since 2000, and download the corrected data. All locations are labelled showing how well they were validated.


As MODIS satellites are nearing the end of their life, any long term fire analysis will have to bridge this sensor change. Using Emberline allows this bridging to be quantified and transparent.
details:
What is Emberline?

Emberline is a web app that turns two NASA satellite fire records into one consistent fire history, from 2000 to today.

Active fire has been detected by MODIS (Terra and Aqua) at 1 km spatial resolution since 2000 and by VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) at 375 m resolution since 2012. As VIIRS detects smaller and cooler fires, and has different overpass times, simply joining the MODIS and VIIRS records produces an apparent increase in fire activity when VIIRS takes over, even when there has been no actual change. We quantified this error in 8 contrasting fire regions across 6 continents. It ranges from +44% in central Portugal to +296% in crop fires in Punjab. This means that there is no single correction factor.

Joining raw VIIRS onto MODIS overstates fire activity in every region, but to varying degrees. Each bar represents a fire region and shows the % overestimation. One factor cannot be applied universally (central Portugal shows 44% overestimation; Punjab shows 296%).

The Emberline algorithm has 4 stages:

1. Preprocessing: Using a Python pipeline we download the FIRMS fire data archives. We unify the sensor data and remove gas flares and industrial sources.

2. Matching: MODIS and VIIRS detections are matched if they occur within the same MODIS pixel footprint. The fires are then put onto a 3 km equal-area grid by local solar day.

3. Correction: We tested 5 different correction methods on years and regions they had never seen, and picked the winner using a rule written before we saw the results. The best performing model, called the bridge model, is a logistic regression that predicts the probability of MODIS detecting each VIIRS fire. This reduces the typical error in a year's total from 17.6% (with 1 scale factor) to 8.0%.

4. Outputting: We produce a unified data set with the corrected values all in one unit, MODIS-equivalent active cell-days, with 90% uncertainty intervals which achieved 92% coverage on unseen years.

The app displays a 3D globe of the last week's fires over NASA satellite imagery. Toggle between MODIS / VIIRS / Corrected to see the gap closing. Filter to any county or area of your choice to display its corrected fire calendar and long-term record. You can compare this season to every season since 2000, view individual fire events and download the data as CSV or GeoJSON.

The global view of the last seven days of fire, over NASA GIBS imagery. You can toggle between MODIS, VIIRS and Corrected in the top left corner. The slider at the bottom allows you to go back to the year 2000 to view fires over time.

What are the Benefits?

  • An artificial trend is removed. Ranked by uncorrected fire size, 19 or 20 of the top 20 largest fires start after 2012 in every study region. This would suggest increasing fire sizes. However, ranked by corrected size, only 10 to 16 of the top 20 start after 2012, close to the 11.5 we would expect by chance. For example, in the Texas Panhandle 2024 is the worst year since 2000 based on the uncorrected data, but the corrected data ranks it below 2005 and 2008.
  • All numbers show their error, and the app shows where the correction is well validated and where it is not.
  • No cost, quick, no account needed. It can be used in any browser, doesn't require a server, fits the width of a phone, and all figures link back to the method and script that generated the

The gap and the correction (Texas Panhandle). Blue = MODIS. Orange dashed = uncorrected VIIRS data joined on. White = corrected data from Emberline, with its 90% uncertainty band shown after 2022.

What is the impact?

The long-term fire record will now depend on VIIRS alone. Suomi NPP ceased providing FIRMS fire data on 2nd November 2026. The MODIS science collection is being ended by NASA, and both MODIS satellites are drifting. In 2026, Terra passes over the Texas Panhandle 99 minutes earlier than it did in its reference years and Aqua passes over 106 minutes later.

State forest services, county emergency managers placing crews, fire-weather forecasters, fire-emissions inventories and land-monitoring NGOs all need to compare current fires against the past 25 years. Emberline provides a single source of consistently collected data with honest error bars, so we know any changes are due to changes in fire, not the satellite.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Data pipeline: pandas, PyArrow, SciPy, scikit-learn and shapely, writing static Parquet and JSON files. One command, make all, rebuilds every number from a clean copy of the code.
  • Web app: Vite, React, MapLibre GL (globe view) and D3.
  • Infrastructure: a GitHub Actions workflow for scheduled data refresh.
  • Hardware: one laptop, with no GPU and no cloud compute.
  • NASA data: FIRMS MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active fire (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), NASA GIBS imagery and fire tiles, MODIS land cover (MCD12Q1), and NASA POWER weather.
  • Validation data: official fire perimeters and burned-area maps from NIFC, CAL FIRE, NSW, Portugal's ICNF and Canada's NBAC.
  • AI: Claude (via Claude Code) wrote most of the code and analysis.

How is our project creative?

  • It measures the problem before fixing it. Instead of assuming one correction works everywhere, we measured how badly the naive join misleads in each fire region and showed the error varies about sevenfold.
  • It holds the sensor count constant. After 2022, exactly one VIIRS satellite carries the record, so adding new satellites can never inflate it.
  • It counts area, not pixels. The equal-area grid means a count in Punjab and a count in Canada are directly comparable.
  • It tests itself like a scientific study. Every hypothesis was written down before testing, a second implementation built only from our method document matched all 148 core results, and our scroll stories replay six real fires (including Smokehouse Creek, the largest wildfire in Texas history) against official perimeters.
  • It publishes its failures. Of 13 candidate findings, 8 failed, and the app lists every one.

Emberline's Map view of the Texas Panhandle, the area where the Smokehouse Creek fire burned in 2024. Each orange square shows a 3 km cell where satellites spotted fire on the chosen day. The buttons switch between the corrected data, just MODIS, just VIIRS, or both.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Scientific honesty. We never show a number without its error, and we hide uncertainty ranges that failed their own coverage test rather than display false confidence. Our "unusual activity" flag is explicitly labeled as not an early warning, because retrospective tests showed it can't predict fires.
  • Reliability. Static hosting means nothing can go down during judging or a fire season, and outage days in the satellite data are detected so they're never read as "no fire".
  • Satellite succession. NOAA-20 carries the record today, and the design adds future satellites as new rows in the benchmark rather than requiring a rebuild.
  • Accessibility. Colorblind-safe palettes, phone layout, keyboard navigation, and plain-language explanations for non-experts.
  • Limits stated plainly. Detections are not burned area, clouds and smoke hide fire, the worldwide correction passes validation in only 2 of 8 held-out regions, and the current year is near-real-time data that will be revised. Emberline is not for life-safety decisions and is not a NASA product. All data sources are credited.
